title: Establish AI SecOps Foundations and Operational Readiness
intro: Building the operational foundations for secure AI: living by least privilege and separation of duties in day-to-day operations; defining roles such as model and data owners; setting release requirements, including human override baselines and reject rate thresholds; preparing playbooks, runbooks and tabletop exercises for incidents such as data poisoning and model tampering; and controlling configuration, automated model updates and drift.
objectives: Apply least privilege, separation of duties and other core principles to AI operations, including emergency changes
Define operational roles, RACI and decision rights for model owners, data owners, MLOps, SecOps and human overseers
Set release requirements, including human override baselines and two-sided reject rate thresholds linked to actions
Prepare AI playbooks and runbooks, and run tabletop exercises for scenarios such as data poisoning and model tampering
Manage AI configuration as code, govern automated model updates, and detect configuration drift

sections.title: Core security principles in AI operations

scenes.title: Principles under pressure
scenes.sub: Core security principles in AI operations
scenes.say: Design principles only protect you if day-to-day operations live by them. Least privilege and separation of duties have to survive on-call rotas, urgent fixes and late-night incidents. | This video covers the core security principles in AI operations, and how to keep them when the pressure is on.

scenes.title: Principles in AI operations

items.d: No standing access; elevate when needed
New models and agents start restricted

scenes.say: Six principles anchor AI operations. | Least privilege in production: no standing administrative access, with elevation only when a task requires it. | Separation of duties: the person who writes a change, the person who approves it, and the pipeline that deploys it are separate. | Defence in depth: guardrails, monitoring and tested recovery, so no single failure is fatal. | Secure defaults: new models, agents and tools start with restricted access. | Fail safe: when a safety or security control breaks, it fails closed. | And accountability: every operational action is attributable to a person or identity, and logged.

scenes.title: When pressure meets principle
rows: Edit the prompt live in production
Deploy with broad access, tighten later
Restricted by default, widened on approval
The team watches its own system
scenes.say: The test of a principle is what happens under pressure. | For an urgent fix, the shortcut is to edit the prompt directly in production. The principled option is an emergency change that still goes through the pipeline. | During an incident, the shortcut is a shared administrator login. The principled option is break-glass access that is logged and reviewed. | For a new model, the shortcut is to deploy with broad access and tighten later, which rarely happens. The principled option is to start restricted and widen on approval. | And for monitoring, the shortcut is letting the team watch its own system. The principled option gives the security operations centre independent visibility.

scenes.title: An emergency change, done safely
scenes.say: Here is how an emergency change keeps its principles. An urgent issue appears: say, an assistant producing harmful outputs in production. | An emergency change request is logged, even if it takes two minutes to write. | Approval comes quickly from someone with pre-agreed on-call authority, not from a full change board. | The fix is deployed through the normal pipeline, so it is tested, signed and recorded, rather than typed into a live console. | Within a day, a post-implementation review checks that the change was right and complete. | And the registry, configuration baseline and documentation are updated, so the emergency fix doesn’t become invisible drift.

items: No standing production access; separate author, approver, deployer
Defence in depth, secure defaults, fail safe, accountability
Pressure is the real test: use emergency paths, not shortcuts
Emergency changes: logged, fast-approved, pipelined, reviewed
scenes.say: To recap. | Hold no standing production access, and keep the author, approver and deployer of changes separate. | Apply defence in depth, secure defaults, fail-safe behaviour and accountability. | Pressure is the real test of principles, so provide fast, controlled emergency paths instead of shortcuts. | And make emergency changes logged, quickly approved, deployed through the pipeline and reviewed afterwards.

blocks.md:
### Principles in practice
| Principle | In AI operations |
|---|---|
| **Least privilege** | Zero standing access to production models, weights, prompts, guardrails and training data; just-in-time elevation (Module 4.6); on-call engineers get only the rights their runbooks need |
| **Separation of duties** | Change authors don’t approve their own changes; deployments run through pipelines with their own identities; the team operating a model isn’t the only team monitoring it |
| **Defence in depth** | Guardrails, authorisation outside the model, monitoring, rate limits, rollback and backups together |
| **Secure defaults** | New models, agents, tools and environments start with minimal permissions, logging on, and outbound access off |
| **Fail safe** | Moderation, DLP and authorisation fail closed; agents stop and escalate on errors (Modules 3.6 and 4.4) |
| **Accountability** | Unique identities for people and agents; every change and privileged action logged (Module 4.5) |
| **Continuous verification** | Configurations, permissions and behaviour checked continuously, not just at release (Section 5) |

### An operational separation-of-duties matrix
Decide in advance who may perform each sensitive operation, and which combinations are forbidden:
- **Deploying a model** (platform team, through the pipeline) versus **approving it** (risk owner).
- **Changing prompts or guardrails** (product team, through change control) versus **changing detection rules** (security operations).
- **Accessing weights or training data** (just-in-time, with approval) versus **administering the identity system**.
- **Running incident containment** (on-call engineer) versus **closing the incident** (incident lead, after review).

### Emergency changes
Emergencies need speed, not exceptions to accountability. Define an **emergency change path** in advance: a minimal logged request, pre-authorised approvers, deployment through the pipeline, and a review within a set time (often 24 to 72 hours). Changes made outside it, such as live edits in a console, should trigger drift alerts (Section 5).

### Framework anchors
The NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 functions (Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover) apply to AI operations as to any other. ISO/IEC 27001 Annex A includes operational controls for change management (8.32), configuration management (8.9), logging (8.15) and monitoring (8.16), which extend naturally to models, prompts and guardrails.

blocks.title: Operations principle questions
blocks.md: Under time pressure, the best answer still keeps **accountability and control**: an **emergency change path**, **break-glass** access, deployment **through the pipeline**, and a **review afterwards**. Answers that skip logging or approval "because it’s urgent" are traps.

q.q: On a Friday night, a production assistant starts giving customers dangerous advice. The on-call engineer can either edit the system prompt live in the admin console or raise an emergency change. What should happen?
o: Edit the prompt live, because customer safety outweighs any process, and document the change on Monday
Use the emergency change path: logged, fast approval, deploy via the pipeline, review afterwards
Wait until Monday’s change board, because all prompt changes need full approval first
Switch off monitoring for the weekend, so the alerts don’t distract the on-call engineer
q.why: The emergency path delivers speed with accountability: the fix is approved, tested, recorded and reviewed. Live edits bypass testing and records, waiting leaves customers at risk, and disabling monitoring removes visibility.

blocks.title: Who does what when AI is live

scenes.title: Who does what when AI is live
scenes.say: When an AI system misbehaves at three in the morning, nobody should be asking who owns it, who can switch it off, or who tells the regulator. | This video covers the operational roles and responsibilities that keep AI systems running safely.

scenes.title: Operational roles

items.d: Accountable for the model in production
Accountable for data the model uses

scenes.say: Six roles matter most once AI is live. | The model owner, usually in the business, is accountable for the model in production: its use, its outcomes and decisions to restrict or retire it. | The data owner is accountable for the data the model uses, including training, retrieval and logs. | MLOps and platform engineers run the pipelines and serving infrastructure, and carry out rollbacks. | Security operations monitors, detects and responds to threats. | Risk and compliance provide oversight, reporting and the link to regulators. | And human overseers review outputs, override the AI when it is wrong, and escalate concerns.

scenes.title: Who does what in an AI incident
scenes.say: A responsibility matrix makes roles concrete. Here is part of one for an AI incident. | Detecting a poisoning signal is security operations’ responsibility. MLOps is consulted, and the model owner is informed. | Rolling back the model is carried out by MLOps, with security consulted, and the decision belongs to the model owner. | Notifying customers or regulators is the model owner’s decision, made with legal and compliance, while security advises. | And tuning the detection rules afterwards falls back to security operations, consulting MLOps.

scenes.title: Making roles work in practice
scenes.say: Six practices turn role definitions into reality. | Assign named people, not just team names. | Give every role deputies and on-call rotas, so someone is reachable at any hour. | Record roles centrally, in the model registry and the runbooks. | Agree decision rights in advance, especially who may switch off or restrict a model without waiting for permission. | Train people and exercise the roles together. | And review assignments after reorganisations, staff changes and incidents.

items: Model owner, data owner, MLOps, SecOps, risk, human overseers
Use a RACI so responsibility and accountability are explicit
Named people, deputies and on-call cover
Pre-agree who may stop or restrict a model
scenes.say: To recap. | The key operational roles are the model owner, data owner, MLOps and platform engineers, security operations, risk and compliance, and human overseers. | Use a responsibility matrix, so it is clear who does the work and who decides. | Assign named people, with deputies and on-call cover. | And agree in advance who may stop or restrict a model, so nobody hesitates in a crisis.

blocks.md:
### Roles and responsibilities
| Role | Operational responsibilities |
|---|---|
| **Model owner** | Accountable for the model in production: approves releases and rollbacks, accepts residual risk, decides on restriction or retirement, owns external communication decisions with legal |
| **Technical owner** | Day-to-day health of the model: performance, monitoring plan, fixes and retraining |
| **Data owner** | Accountable for training, retrieval and log data: approves uses, access and retention; leads data aspects of incidents such as poisoning or leakage (Module 3.1 covers data owners, stewards and custodians) |
| **MLOps and platform engineering** | Pipelines, serving, scaling, configuration management, rollback and recovery |
| **Security operations (SOC)** | AI telemetry, detection rules, triage, containment actions, threat intelligence (Modules 5.2 to 5.5) |
| **AI incident lead** | Coordinates response across teams; owns the incident timeline and decisions log |
| **Risk, compliance and legal** | Oversight, regulatory notifications, contractual obligations, evidence preservation |
| **Human overseers** | Review and override AI outputs in operation; report anomalies (EU AI Act Articles 14 and 26 require competent, trained people with authority for high-risk systems) |
| **Providers and vendors** | Their share of responsibilities under the shared responsibility model (Module 2.5) |

### RACI in practice
**Responsible** people do the work; the **accountable** person makes the decision and answers for it (only one per task); **consulted** people give input; **informed** people are kept up to date. Build a RACI for each critical activity: release, monitoring, rollback, incident containment, external notification, retraining and retirement.

### Decision rights
The most important decision to agree in advance is **who may stop or restrict an AI system** in an emergency. On-call engineers should be able to take pre-approved containment actions, such as switching to a fallback, restricting features or disabling an agent, without waiting for a meeting, with the model owner informed immediately.

pairs: Deciding to retire a credit-scoring model

Data owner
Executing the rollback to the previous model version
MLOps / platform team
Writing a detection rule for prompt injection attempts

blocks.title: Role questions
blocks.md: Remember the difference between **responsible** (does the work) and **accountable** (owns the decision). In AI operations, the **model owner** is usually accountable for production decisions, while MLOps and the SOC are responsible for executing them. Shared or unclear ownership is a finding in itself.

q.q: During an incident, MLOps engineers want to roll back a customer-facing model, but nobody is sure who may authorise it, and the decision waits two hours. What should be fixed?
o: Give every engineer authority to change any production model whenever they think it necessary
Define decision rights in advance, including pre-approved containment actions for on-call staff
Require every rollback to be approved by the full executive committee in future
Remove the rollback option, so that engineers aren’t faced with this decision again
q.why: Pre-agreed decision rights and pre-approved containment let on-call staff act quickly within limits, with the model owner accountable. Unlimited authority removes control, executive approval is too slow, and removing rollback removes recovery.

sections.title: Release requirements: override baselines and reject rate thresholds

scenes.title: Ready for production?
scenes.sub: Release requirements, override baselines and reject rate thresholds
scenes.say: Before an AI system goes live, operations needs agreed answers to three questions: what does good look like, what does bad look like, and when do we stop? | This video covers release requirements, including human override baselines and reject rate thresholds.

scenes.title: Operational release requirements
scenes.say: An operational release checklist covers six things. | Evaluations passed: quality, safety, fairness and security suites, against agreed thresholds. | Security sign-off, with red-team findings fixed or formally accepted by the risk owner. | Monitoring live: telemetry flowing, alerts configured and dashboards built, before the first user arrives. | Runbooks written and on-call staff trained. | Rollback tested, with the previous version ready to restore. | And operational thresholds agreed, such as human override rates, reject rates and error rates, with the action each breach triggers.

scenes.title: Human override rate as a health signal
scenes.yLabel: Illustrative share of AI recommendations overridden by reviewers, per week

annot.text: Upper threshold: is the model degrading?
Lower threshold: are reviewers still checking?

scenes.say: A human override baseline records how often reviewers overrule the AI when everything is working normally. In this illustrative chart it sits at around ten per cent. | An upper threshold catches the obvious problem: when overrides jump, as in weeks seven and eight, the model may be degrading, or the population may have changed. | A lower threshold catches the less obvious one: when overrides fall towards zero, as in weeks eleven and twelve, reviewers may have stopped checking and started rubber-stamping. That is automation bias, and it removes the human safeguard silently.

scenes.title: Reject rates: too high or too low
rows: Filter failing, or attacks getting through
scenes.say: Reject rate thresholds work in both directions, because either extreme signals a problem. | If the guardrail block rate is too high, legitimate users are being blocked and will drift to unapproved tools. Too low, and the filter may have failed, or attacks may be slipping through. | If the model refuses too often, it is unusable and the policy may be too strict. If refusals drop sharply, its safety behaviour may have been eroded, for example by a bad update. | And if output validation rejects too much, the model or prompt may be broken. If it rejects almost nothing, check that validation is still running at all.

items: Release only with evaluations, sign-off, monitoring, runbooks and rollback
Baseline human override rates; alert on rises and falls
Set reject rate thresholds in both directions
Link every threshold to a defined action
scenes.say: To recap. | Release only when evaluations, security sign-off, monitoring, runbooks and tested rollback are all in place. | Baseline the human override rate, and alert when it rises or falls outside its band. | Set reject rate thresholds in both directions for guardrails, refusals and output validation. | And link every threshold to a defined action, such as investigating, restricting or rolling back.

blocks.md:
### A production readiness review
| Area | Typical requirement |
|---|---|
| **Evaluation** | Quality, safety, fairness and security suites passed against agreed thresholds (Modules 3.5 and 4.4) |
| **Security** | Threat model current; red-team findings fixed or accepted by the risk owner (Domain 6) |
| **Monitoring** | Telemetry, detections, dashboards and alert routing live (Module 5.2) |
| **Operations** | Runbooks, on-call rota, escalation paths and decision rights (Section 2) |
| **Resilience** | Rollback tested; fallbacks and degradation paths defined (Module 3.6) |
| **Thresholds** | Operational limits with defined actions, recorded in the monitoring plan |
| **Approval** | Sign-off by the model owner in line with the risk tier |

### Human override baselines
In systems with a human in or on the loop, the **override rate** (how often reviewers reject or change the AI’s output) is a key operational signal.
- **Measure a baseline** during pilots and early operation, by decision type and reviewer group.
- **Upper threshold:** rising overrides suggest model degradation, drift or a change in the population (Module 3.5).
- **Lower threshold:** overrides near zero, very fast approvals, or identical decisions across reviewers suggest **automation bias** and rubber-stamping. The EU AI Act (Article 14) requires human oversight measures that help overseers stay aware of the tendency to over-rely on AI output, and to be able to decide not to use it or to override it.
- **Responses:** investigate the model, sample decisions for audit, refresh reviewer training, add friction such as requiring reasons, and rotate reviewers.

### Reject rate thresholds
Track, with thresholds in both directions:
- **Guardrail block rates** on inputs and outputs (Module 4.4).
- **Model refusal rates** and abstentions.
- **Output validation failures** (schema, DLP, grounding checks).
- **Escalation rates** to humans, and **error and time-out rates**.

Set initial bands from pilot data, review them after changes, and tie each breach to an action: investigate, restrict use, switch to a fallback or roll back (Module 3.5). Record thresholds and actions in the monitoring plan so on-call staff don’t have to improvise.

blocks.title: The perfect approval rate
blocks.md: A bank uses an AI model to recommend whether to approve small-business loans, with credit officers reviewing every recommendation. During the pilot, officers overrode about 12% of recommendations. Six months later, the override rate is 0.4%, the average review takes eleven seconds, and managers are pleased with the efficiency.

q.q: What is the MOST appropriate response?
o: Celebrate the result, because the model has clearly become more accurate over time
Treat it as a possible automation-bias signal: audit a sample of decisions and strengthen oversight
Remove the human review step, since officers are agreeing with the model almost every single time
Increase the number of applications each officer reviews, to make use of the extra time
q.why: An override rate far below baseline with very short reviews suggests rubber-stamping, not necessarily a better model. Sampling decisions shows which is true, and oversight measures restore meaningful review. Removing or diluting review would make any problem worse.

blocks.title: Release threshold questions
blocks.md: Thresholds should have **two sides** and **defined actions**. A falling override rate or a falling block rate isn’t automatically good news: it may mean **automation bias** or a **failing control**. The best answers investigate before celebrating.

q.q: After a provider updates the underlying model, a customer chatbot’s refusal rate on known harmful test prompts falls from 98% to 70%. What should the operational thresholds trigger?
o: Nothing, because a lower refusal rate means the chatbot is more helpful to customers
The defined action for a safety breach, such as restricting use or rolling back, then investigating
A request to the provider to explain its update in its next quarterly business review
An adjustment to the threshold, so that 70% becomes the new normal for the chatbot
q.why: A sharp fall in refusals of harmful prompts signals eroded safety behaviour, so the pre-agreed action applies: restrict or roll back, then investigate. Calling it helpfulness, waiting for a business review or moving the threshold all leave users exposed.

scenes.title: Rehearsing the bad day
scenes.say: Nobody wants to work out for the first time, mid-incident, how to tell whether a model has been poisoned, or how to roll back a tampered one. | This video covers the operational playbooks, runbooks and tabletop exercises that prepare teams for AI incidents.

scenes.title: Playbooks and runbooks
rows: What to do, and who decides
Exactly how to do one task
Roll back to the last signed model
scenes.say: Playbooks and runbooks work together. | A playbook describes what to do in a type of incident, and who decides. A runbook describes exactly how to carry out one task. | Playbooks are for incident leads and managers. Runbooks are for the engineers on call. | For example, a playbook covers suspected training data poisoning, and it calls a runbook for rolling back to the last signed model. | Playbooks contain triggers, roles, decision points and communications. Runbooks contain commands, checks and the results to expect at each step.

scenes.title: AI playbooks to have ready
scenes.say: Six AI playbooks cover most scenarios. | Data poisoning: suspicious data, or an unexplained shift in model behaviour. | Model tampering or theft: weights altered in storage, or copied out. | Prompt injection abuse: jailbreaks, or agents hijacked through the content they read. | Sensitive data leakage through outputs. | Agent misbehaviour: harmful, unauthorised or runaway actions. | And provider failure: an outage, or an update that makes a hosted model unsafe.

scenes.title: Outline of a data poisoning playbook
scenes.say: Here is the outline of a data poisoning playbook. It starts with a signal: unexplained drift, failing canary tests, a backdoor-like trigger found by red teamers, or a report from a data supplier. | Triage uses lineage to scope the problem: which datasets are affected, and which models were trained on them. | Containment freezes the affected pipelines and rolls back to the last model trained before the suspect data arrived. | Investigation compares data versions and reviews access logs, to find what changed, when and by whom. | Eradication removes or repairs the bad data, and retrains from clean sources. | And recovery restores service with extra monitoring, followed by a review that updates the playbook itself.

scenes.title: Running a useful tabletop exercise
scenes.say: A tabletop exercise walks the team through an incident in a meeting room, without touching production. Six ingredients make it useful. | A realistic scenario based on your own systems, such as tampered weights found in the model registry. | Every role present: security operations, MLOps, data science, the model owner, legal and communications. | Injects: new facts introduced during the exercise, such as a journalist’s call or evidence the backdoor has been live for a month. | Real time pressure, including regulatory notification clocks. | A careful record of gaps: missing runbooks, unclear decision rights, absent logs. | And actions with owners and dates, followed through to completion.

items: Playbooks decide and coordinate; runbooks execute
Prepare for poisoning, tampering, injection, leakage, agents, providers
Use lineage to scope; roll back to a clean, signed model
Exercise with all roles, injects and time pressure; close the gaps
scenes.say: To recap. | Playbooks set out decisions and coordination; runbooks give the exact steps. | Prepare playbooks for poisoning, tampering, injection, leakage, agent misbehaviour and provider failure. | In poisoning cases, use lineage to scope the damage, and roll back to a clean, signed model. | And exercise the plans with every role, realistic injects and time pressure, then close the gaps you find.

blocks.md:
### Playbook contents
A good AI incident playbook includes:
- **Triggers and indicators:** what starts it (detections, reports, threshold breaches).
- **Severity criteria** and the AI-specific triage taxonomy (Module 5.5).
- **Roles and decision rights**, including who can contain without further approval (Section 2).
- **Decision points:** for example, *roll back or restrict? retrain or unlearn? notify now or after investigation?*
- **Containment options** with links to runbooks: switch to fallback, disable an agent, freeze a pipeline, revoke keys, block a tool.
- **Evidence to preserve:** model weights and versions, configurations, prompts, logs, dataset snapshots (Module 5.5).
- **Communications:** internal, customer and regulatory, with clocks such as GDPR’s 72 hours for personal data breaches, NIS2’s 24-hour early warning, and EU AI Act serious incident reporting for high-risk systems.

### Runbooks
Runbooks are **specific, tested and current**: model rollback to the last signed version; registry quarantine of a suspect model; revoking and rotating model provider keys; disabling an agent identity; freezing training pipelines; restoring a vector index from a clean snapshot. Automate the safe ones in SOAR (Module 5.2), keep a human approval step for destructive actions, and test them in game days (Module 4.4).

### Tabletop exercises
- Follow an exercise programme (NIST SP 800-84 describes test, training and exercise programmes for IT plans).
- Start with discussion-based tabletops, then progress to functional exercises in test environments.
- Useful AI scenarios: poisoned data from a labelling vendor; tampered weights in the registry; an agent leaking data after reading a malicious email; theft of a fine-tuned model; a provider update that removes safety behaviour; a deepfake of an executive used to authorise a payment.
- Collaborate across organisations where possible: in 2024, CISA’s Joint Cyber Defense Collaborative ran an AI-focused tabletop exercise with industry partners, and in January 2025 it published an AI Cybersecurity Collaboration Playbook for sharing information about AI incidents.
- After each exercise, update playbooks and runbooks, and track actions to closure.

blocks.title: Preparation questions
blocks.md: Look for preparation that is **specific to AI** (lineage-based scoping, rollback to signed models, evidence such as weights and dataset snapshots), **exercised** with all roles, and **improved** after each exercise. A generic IT incident plan with no AI scenarios is a gap.

q.q: A tabletop exercise on model tampering reveals that nobody knows how to confirm whether production weights match the approved version. What is the BEST follow-up?
o: Record the finding in the exercise report, and repeat exactly the same exercise again next year
Write and test a runbook that checks weights against signed registry hashes; update the playbook
Ask the vendor of the registry tool to provide detailed training to the whole engineering team
Replace the production model with a new one straight away, because it may have been tampered with
q.why: Exercises exist to find and close gaps: a tested verification runbook, referenced in the playbook, fixes this one. Just recording it leaves the gap, vendor training is incomplete, and replacing the model isn’t justified by an exercise finding.

sections.title: Configuration management, automated updates and drift tracking

scenes.title: Keeping AI configuration under control
scenes.sub: Configuration management, automated updates and drift
scenes.say: An AI system’s behaviour depends on much more than its code: the model version, its prompts, its guardrail settings, its retrieval index and its tools. Change any of them, and behaviour changes. | This video covers configuration management for AI, automated model updates, and tracking configuration drift.

scenes.title: What counts as AI configuration
scenes.say: Six layers of configuration shape an AI system’s behaviour. | The model version and its parameters, such as temperature and output limits. | Prompts and templates, including system prompts and examples. | Guardrail policies: filters, thresholds and allow-lists. | Retrieval settings: which index, which embedding model, which sources and filters. | Tools and permissions: which tools agents can call, with which scopes, through which servers. | And the infrastructure underneath: images, scaling and network rules. All of them belong under configuration management.

scenes.title: Configuration as code, with drift detection
scenes.say: The strongest pattern is configuration as code. The desired state of every configuration item lives in version control, where changes are reviewed. | A pipeline applies approved changes, after tests, and records exactly what was deployed. | The running system holds the actual state. | A drift detector continually compares the actual state with the desired state: model versions, prompt hashes, guardrail settings, tool permissions and infrastructure. | When they differ, it alerts, or for high-risk items reverts automatically. | And every change, approved or not, ends up in a change record showing who changed what, and why.

scenes.title: Automated model updates
rows: Pinned versions; retraining makes a candidate
scenes.say: Automated model updates save effort, but only if they are managed. | Unmanaged, a provider moves an alias to a new model, or a retraining pipeline deploys its own output. Managed, versions are pinned, and retraining produces a candidate rather than a release. | Unmanaged, users are the first testers. Managed, evaluation suites gate every release. | Unmanaged, approval is implicit. Managed, approval is proportionate to risk and recorded. | And unmanaged, nobody is sure what to roll back to. Managed, the previous version is always ready.

scenes.title: Configuration drift to watch for

items.d: Network or scaling edited by hand

scenes.say: Six kinds of configuration drift are common in AI systems. | A prompt edited directly in a console, outside change control. | A guardrail threshold quietly loosened to reduce complaints. | A new tool added to an agent, widening its scope without approval. | A provider alias moved, so the model changed underneath you. | A retrieval index rebuilt with new sources or a new embedding model. | And infrastructure changed by hand, such as a network rule opened for testing and never closed.

items: Treat models, prompts, guardrails, retrieval, tools and infra as configuration
Desired state in version control, applied by pipelines
Detect drift continuously; alert or revert by risk
Automated updates: pinned, gated, approved, reversible
scenes.say: To recap. | Treat model versions, prompts, guardrails, retrieval settings, tools and infrastructure as configuration. | Keep the desired state in version control, and apply it only through pipelines. | Detect drift continuously, alerting or reverting according to risk. | And make automated model updates pinned, gated by evaluation, approved and reversible.

blocks.md:
### Configuration management for AI
Security-focused configuration management (described in NIST SP 800-128, and in ISO/IEC 27001 Annex A 8.9) means: identifying **configuration items**, setting **approved baselines**, controlling **changes**, **monitoring** for deviations, and **auditing**. For AI, configuration items include:
- **Model:** provider and pinned version, or registry version and hash; generation parameters.
- **Prompts:** system prompts, templates and examples, versioned and hashed.
- **Guardrails:** classifier versions, thresholds, policies, allow-lists and block-lists.
- **Retrieval:** index version, embedding model, data sources, chunking, filters and top-k settings.
- **Agents:** tools, scopes, MCP servers, budgets and approval rules.
- **Infrastructure:** container images, serving configuration, autoscaling, network and IAM policies.

### Configuration drift
Drift is any difference between the approved baseline and what is actually running. Detect it with:
- **Configuration-as-code reconciliation** (GitOps controllers that compare and restore desired state).
- **Hashes** of prompts, guardrail policies and tool definitions, checked at runtime.
- **Version checks** on models and indexes, including **behavioural canaries**: a fixed set of test prompts run on a schedule to detect hosted-model changes (Module 3.6).
- **Cloud and IaC drift detection** for infrastructure and permissions.

Don’t confuse **configuration drift** (the system was changed) with **model or data drift** (the world changed, Module 1.3). Both matter, and both need monitoring, but they have different causes and fixes.

### Automated model updates
- **Hosted models:** pin dated versions; track deprecation notices; test new versions in shadow or canary before switching (Module 3.5).
- **Continuous training pipelines:** retraining may run automatically, but its output is a **candidate** that must pass evaluation gates and, for higher-risk models, human approval before release.
- **Guardrail and classifier updates** are changes too: test them for false positives and negatives before rollout.
- **Dependencies:** patch serving stacks and libraries through the same pipeline (Module 5.4).
- Keep the **previous version deployable** for rollback, and record every update in the registry.

Configuration drift

blocks.title: Configuration questions
blocks.md: Look for **desired state in version control**, **changes only through pipelines**, **continuous drift detection** and **pinned, gated updates**. If a question describes behaviour changing "with no code change", suspect configuration drift: a prompt, guardrail, index, tool or provider version changed.

q.q: An assistant’s answers suddenly become less accurate and less safe. No code was deployed, but investigation shows its system prompt was edited in the provider’s console last week. Which control would MOST likely have detected this quickly?
o: A quarterly review of all the assistant’s prompts by the product team and its manager
Prompts held as code, with runtime hash checks and alerts on drift from the approved version
A larger evaluation suite, run once before the assistant’s original launch last year
Annual training for all staff on why prompts must never be edited directly in provider consoles
q.why: Treating prompts as configuration items, with hashes compared continuously against the approved baseline, flags unapproved edits within minutes. Quarterly reviews, one-off launch tests and training don’t detect a change when it happens.

quiz.q: What does "no standing access" mean for AI production systems?
o: Nobody is ever allowed to access production models or data for any reason
Privileged rights are granted just in time for each task, then removed again
Access is granted only to engineers who are physically present in the office
Production access is shared through one team account with a strong password
quiz.why: Standing privileges are an easy target. Just-in-time elevation gives engineers the rights they need, only while they need them, with a record of each use.

quiz.q: Which arrangement BEST shows separation of duties for model releases?
o: The data scientist who trained the model also approves and deploys it, to save time
The author, the approver and the deploying pipeline are separate parties
The model is deployed first, and approved afterwards by the author’s manager
The release is approved by whoever is on call when the model is ready
quiz.why: Separating authorship, approval and deployment means no single person can push an unreviewed or malicious change to production.

quiz.q: What should happen after an emergency change has been deployed?
o: Nothing further, because it was approved by the on-call authority at the time
A post-implementation review within a set time, and updated records
It should be reversed automatically after 24 hours unless it is renewed
It should be reported to the regulator as a deviation from process
quiz.why: Emergency changes trade some up-front scrutiny for speed, so a prompt review confirms the change was right, and records keep it from becoming invisible drift.

quiz.q: Who is usually accountable for decisions about an AI model in production, such as restricting or retiring it?
o: The data scientist who originally built and trained the model
The model owner, typically a senior leader in the business
The security operations centre that monitors the model
The cloud provider that hosts the model’s serving infrastructure
quiz.why: The model owner answers for the model’s use and outcomes, so production decisions are theirs, while technical teams carry them out.

quiz.q: In a RACI matrix, what is the difference between responsible and accountable?
o: Responsible people approve the work; accountable people carry it out
Responsible people do the work; one accountable person owns the decision
Responsible people are internal staff; accountable people are vendors
There is no difference; the two terms are interchangeable in RACI
quiz.why: Several people may be responsible for doing the work, but exactly one person is accountable for each decision.

quiz.q: What is a human override baseline?
o: The maximum number of times a reviewer may override the AI in a day
The normal rate at which reviewers overrule AI outputs, measured in pilots
The minimum accuracy a model must reach before human reviewers are allowed to stop checking it
The number of reviewers needed to override a single AI decision
quiz.why: The baseline describes normal behaviour, so upper and lower thresholds around it can reveal model problems or rubber-stamping.

quiz.q: Why might an override rate falling close to zero be a warning sign?
o: It shows that the model has been retrained on too little data
Reviewers may be rubber-stamping outputs because of automation bias
It indicates that the decision threshold was set too high at launch
It proves that the human reviewers are no longer needed
quiz.why: Overrides near zero, especially with very fast reviews, suggest people have stopped checking, which silently removes the human safeguard.

quiz.q: Why should reject rate thresholds be set in both directions?
o: Because regulators require two thresholds for every metric that is monitored
Both too many and too few rejections can signal a real problem
Because a single threshold can’t be displayed on most dashboards
So that the threshold can be adjusted whenever users complain
quiz.why: Too many rejections suggest over-blocking or a broken model; too few suggest a failed control or eroded safety behaviour.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between a playbook and a runbook?
o: Playbooks are written by vendors; runbooks are written in-house
Playbooks cover decisions and roles; runbooks give exact steps for a task
Playbooks are used only in exercises; runbooks are used only in real incidents
A playbook covers technical commands; a runbook covers communications
quiz.why: Playbooks coordinate the response to a type of incident; runbooks are the tested, step-by-step instructions they call on.

quiz.q: What is an inject in a tabletop exercise?
o: A test input sent to a production model during the exercise
New information introduced during the exercise to force decisions
A summary of lessons learned that is circulated after the exercise
A scripted answer that participants read out at each stage
quiz.why: Injects, such as a journalist’s call or new evidence, make the scenario evolve and test how the team decides under pressure.

quiz.q: Which of these is a configuration item for an AI system?
o: How many users signed up for the product in the last month
The system prompt, with its approved version number and hash
The marketing description of the product on the company website
The names of the data scientists who built the first prototype
quiz.why: Anything whose settings shape the system’s behaviour, such as prompts, model versions, guardrails, indexes and tool permissions, is a configuration item.

quiz.q: How does configuration drift differ from model drift?
o: Configuration drift affects only infrastructure; model drift affects only data
Configuration drift means the system was changed; model drift means the world changed
They are the same thing, described by different teams in different ways
Configuration drift is always malicious; model drift is always accidental
quiz.why: Configuration drift is a change to the system itself, such as an edited prompt; model drift comes from changes in the data or environment.

exam.q: An AI platform team uses one shared administrator account for production model changes, so on-call engineers can act quickly at night. An audit finds that nobody can tell who changed a guardrail threshold last month. What is the BEST remediation?
o: Keep the shared account, but change its password every month and limit who knows it
Named individual identities, just-in-time elevation and logged break-glass access
Remove all production access, so that guardrail thresholds can never be changed again
Ask engineers to note their changes in the team chat after each shift
exam.why: Individual identities with just-in-time elevation and logged break-glass access keep speed and restore accountability. Password rotation keeps the account shared, removing all access stops operations, and chat notes are unreliable.

exam.q: A retailer’s recommendation model is found to be using customer purchase data for a purpose customers weren’t told about. The data science team says it only builds models, and the business says the data team approved it. Which gap does this MOST clearly reveal?
o: The model was trained without enough data to produce accurate recommendations
No clear data owner accountable for approving uses of the customer data
The security operations centre failed to detect the misuse in its logs
The company didn’t buy a commercial recommendation engine from a vendor
exam.why: Each side assumes the other approved the use, which shows that nobody is accountable for decisions about the data. A named data owner approves uses, access and retention.

exam.q: A hospital is preparing to release an AI triage assistant. Evaluations have passed and the security review is complete, but no alerts or dashboards exist yet, and the team plans to add them "after go-live". What should the security lead recommend?
o: Release on schedule, because evaluations and the security review were both passed
Delay release until monitoring, alerting and agreed thresholds are in place
Release to all users, but ask clinicians to report any problems they notice
Cancel the project, because the team has shown it can’t be trusted with AI
exam.why: Monitoring is a release requirement: without it, degradation or attacks would go unnoticed in a high-impact setting. Releasing anyway relies on luck or users, and cancelling is disproportionate.

exam.q: Three months after launch, a content moderation guardrail’s block rate drops from 4% of inputs to 0.1% overnight, with no change in traffic. What is the MOST likely explanation to investigate first?
o: Users have become more polite, so fewer of their inputs now need to be blocked
The guardrail may have failed, or been disabled or misconfigured by a change
Attackers have given up trying to misuse the system after launch
The model provider has improved the model, so the guardrail is no longer needed
exam.why: A sudden fall with stable traffic points to a broken or altered control, which is why reject rate thresholds have a lower bound. Behaviour rarely changes overnight like this.

exam.q: A company has a detailed general IT incident response plan. It is adopting several AI agents that can act on customer accounts. During a review, which gap is MOST important to address?
o: The plan’s contact list hasn’t been updated with the AI vendor’s sales team
No AI-specific playbooks, such as agent misbehaviour, or exercises to test them
The plan is stored as a PDF instead of in a collaborative online editor
The plan doesn’t include a glossary explaining AI terms for new staff
exam.why: AI incidents need specific triggers, containment such as disabling agents, and evidence such as tool-call logs, and teams must practise them. The other gaps are minor.

exam.q: During a tabletop exercise on training data poisoning, participants realise they can’t identify which production models were trained on the suspect dataset. What should the organisation do as a result?
o: Retrain every production model immediately, in case any of them were affected
Implement data and model lineage tracking, and add lineage checks to the playbook
Stop running tabletop exercises, because they create unnecessary concern among staff
Ask data scientists to keep personal notes of the datasets used for each model
exam.why: Lineage lets responders scope a poisoning incident quickly, and the playbook should use it. Retraining everything is disproportionate, stopping exercises hides gaps, and personal notes are unreliable.

exam.q: A financial firm calls a hosted LLM through the provider’s "latest" model alias. After a provider update, output formats change and a downstream payment workflow breaks. Which control would BEST have prevented this?
o: Asking the provider to give at least a week’s notice before changing any model
Pinning a dated model version, and testing each new version before switching
Building a second workflow that can be used whenever the first one breaks
Monitoring the provider’s status page for announcements of model releases
exam.why: A pinned version can’t change underneath the workflow, and new versions are adopted only after testing. Notice periods and status pages don’t stop the change, and a second workflow adds cost without fixing the cause.

exam.q: A retraining pipeline automatically deploys a new fraud model every night if training completes without errors. Which change BEST reduces the risk of this process?
o: Run the retraining pipeline weekly instead of nightly, so there are fewer releases
Treat each retrained model as a candidate gated by evaluations and approval
Let the pipeline deploy, but email the data science team a summary each morning
Disable automated retraining, and retrain manually only once a year
exam.why: Finishing without errors doesn’t mean a model is good or safe. Evaluation gates and risk-based approval keep the automation while stopping poor or poisoned models reaching production.
